lessons.title: Functions of Slag in Smelting
lessons.body:
Slag is not wasteâit is a tool. In smelting, slag does four critical jobs. First, it collects impurities like silica, alumina, and sulfur from the metal, allowing you to pour clean metal. Second, it protects the metal from oxidation by forming a blanket that keeps air away. Third, it helps transfer heat from the furnace to the metal. Fourth, it can be used to control the furnace temperature and chemistry.

In Africa, many small-scale smelters use locally available materials. For example, in a typical copper smelting operation in Zambia, the charge might include copper oxide ore, coke, and silica sand. The silica sand is added to form slag with iron oxides. Without enough silica, the slag becomes too thick and traps metal droplets, reducing recovery. A good slag has a composition that is fluid at smelting temperature, usually 1200â1300Â°C for copper, and separates easily from the metal.

You can test slag function by watching the slag as it taps from the furnace. If it flows like honey and forms a glassy solid when cool, it is working. If it is pasty or contains visible metal prills, you need to adjust the charge. A simple field test: take a slag sample, crush it, and pan it. If you see shiny metal particles, your slag is not doing its job. Adjust by adding more silica (sand) or lime (limestone) depending on the slagâs acidity.

Remember, slag also affects furnace lining life. A very acidic slag (high silica) can eat away basic refractory bricks. In Africa, many furnaces use clay or locally made bricks, so keeping slag composition balanced is key to avoiding frequent rebuilds. Aim for a slag that is slightly acidic to neutral, with a silica-to-iron ratio around 1:1 to 1.5:1 for copper smelting.

lessons.title: Slag Composition and Properties
lessons.body:
Slag is mostly silica (SiO2), iron oxide (FeO), lime (CaO), and alumina (Al2O3). These four make up over 90% of most smelting slags. The exact mix depends on your ore and flux. For example, a typical copper slag in Africa might contain 40% SiO2, 35% FeO, 10% CaO, and 5% Al2O3. The rest is minor elements like sulfur, copper, and zinc.

Key properties to watch: melting point, density, and viscosity. Melting point is the temperature at which slag becomes liquid. Most smelting slags melt between 1100Â°C and 1300Â°C. You can estimate melting point by looking at the slagâs color when hotâbright orange is around 1200Â°C, yellow-white is 1400Â°C. Density matters because slag must float on metal. Molten slag density is typically 2.5â3.0 g/cmÂ³, while copper is 8.9 g/cmÂ³ and iron is 7.8 g/cmÂ³. That difference allows separation.

Viscosity is how thick the slag is. It depends on temperature and composition. High silica makes slag thick; adding lime or iron oxide makes it thinner. In practice, you want slag that flows like cooking oil at smelting temperature. If it is too thick, metal droplets get trapped. If too thin, it may corrode the furnace walls.

You can measure slag properties with simple tools. A slag sample can be cooled and examined for color and texture. A glassy, dark slag is usually good. A stony, dull slag may have high alumina or lime. Use a steel rod to stir the slag in the furnaceâif it coats the rod easily, it is too thick. Adjust by adding flux: sand for acidic ores, limestone for basic ores. Always keep records of your charge and slag appearance so you can repeat good batches.

lessons.title: Slag Viscosity and Fluidity
lessons.body:
Viscosity is the resistance of slag to flow. In smelting, you need slag that is fluid enough to tap easily and let metal droplets settle. Think of it like honey versus water. Too thick (high viscosity) and the slag won't drain, trapping metal. Too thin (low viscosity) and it may splash and erode furnace lining.

Temperature is the biggest control. For every 50Â°C increase, slag viscosity drops by about half. So if your slag is thick, first try increasing furnace temperature. In a typical charcoal-fired furnace in Africa, you can raise temperature by adding more air with a blower or using drier, denser charcoal. But don't overheatâabove 1400Â°C, you waste fuel and risk damaging the furnace.

Composition also matters. Silica (SiO2) increases viscosity. Iron oxide (FeO) and lime (CaO) decrease it. A good rule: keep silica between 35% and 45%, and lime between 5% and 15%. If your slag is too thick, add iron oxide (mill scale or rust) or lime (limestone). If too thin, add silica sand. In many African smelters, the ore itself provides iron, so you may only need to add sand or limestone.

You can test viscosity with a simple slag stick. Dip a dry wooden stick into the slag for 2 seconds. If the slag coats the stick thinly and drips off, viscosity is good. If it forms a thick glob, it's too viscous. Another test: pour a small slag sample onto a metal plate. It should spread to a thin pancake, not stay as a blob. Adjust your charge based on these tests. Keep a log of temperature, charge, and slag behavior to learn what works for your ore.

lessons.title: Metal-Slag Separation
lessons.body:
After smelting, you must separate metal from slag. This happens in the furnace and during tapping. Good separation means more metal recovery and cleaner slag. The key is density difference: metal is heavier and sinks, slag floats. But if slag is too viscous or too little time is given, metal droplets get trapped.

In practice, you need a settling period. After the charge is fully molten, stop adding air and let the furnace rest for 15â30 minutes. This allows metal droplets to sink. In African furnaces, this is often done by closing the air supply and letting the furnace cool slightly. The metal collects at the bottom, slag on top. Then you tap the slag first, then the metal.

Tapping is critical. Use a tapping hole at the slag level to drain slag, then a lower hole for metal. If you only have one tap hole, tilt the furnace carefully. Let the slag flow out firstâit's lighter and will come out first if you tap from the top. Then tap the metal. If you see slag mixed with metal, stop and let it settle more.

Tools: a tapping rod (steel), a slag pot (cast iron or steel), and a metal mold. Always preheat the tapping rod and pots to avoid chilling the slag. In many small operations in Africa, a simple clay-lined pit serves as a slag pot. But be carefulâmolten slag can explode if it hits water. Keep the area dry.

After tapping, let the slag cool. You can break it open to check for trapped metal. If you see shiny prills, crush the slag and pan it to recover metal. This is common in artisanal copper and tin smelting. Good separation can recover over 90% of metal; poor separation may lose 20% or more in slag.

lessons.title: Slag Handling and Utilization
lessons.body:
Once slag is tapped and cooled, it becomes a solid, glassy material. Don't just throw it awayâit has uses. In Africa, slag can be used for road base, concrete aggregate, and even as a soil amendment if it contains lime. But first, you must handle it safely.

Cooling: Never cool slag with water while it's hot. It can explode into steam. Let it air-cool in a dry pit or on a steel plate. Once solid, it can be broken with a sledgehammer. Wear safety glasses, gloves, and bootsâslag shards are sharp.

Storage: Store slag in a dry area. If it gets wet, it may leach metals like copper or zinc, which can contaminate groundwater. In many African smelters, slag is piled outside. Cover it with a tarp or store under a roof if possible. Test the slag for heavy metals if you plan to use it near water sources.

Utilization: Crushed slag makes excellent road fill because it is hard and angular. It can also be used as aggregate in concrete blocks. In some countries, slag is used to make mineral wool for insulation. If your slag contains high lime (over 20% CaO), it can be ground and used to neutralize acidic soils. But check for heavy metals firstâcopper slag may contain arsenic or lead.

Selling slag: In some regions, there is a market for slag as a construction material. You can sell it to local builders or road contractors. But you need consistent quality. Keep your slag cleanâdon't mix it with garbage or furnace ash. If you produce a lot, consider setting up a small crushing and screening operation. This adds value and reduces waste.

lessons.title: Environmental Aspects of Slag Disposal
lessons.body:
Slag can be a pollution source if not managed. The main risks are heavy metals (lead, arsenic, cadmium) and sulfur. When slag is exposed to rain, these elements can leach into groundwater. In Africa, where many communities rely on wells and rivers, this is serious.

First, know your slag. Test it for heavy metals. Simple field tests are available, but a lab test is best. If your slag contains more than 1% lead or 0.5% arsenic, it is hazardous. Do not use it near water or homes. Instead, store it in a lined pit with a clay or plastic liner to prevent leaching. Cover it to keep rain out.

Second, reduce slag generation. Better smelting practices mean less slag per ton of metal. For example, optimizing flux addition can reduce slag volume by 10â20%. Also, recover metal from slag by crushing and panning. This reduces the metal content in slag, making it less hazardous.

Third, disposal options. If slag is non-hazardous, you can use it for road base or concrete. If hazardous, you must dispose of it in a controlled landfill. In many African countries, regulations are weak, but you should still act responsibly. Dig a pit away from water sources, line it with clay, and bury the slag. After filling, cover with soil and plant grass.

Fourth, protect workers. Slag dust can cause lung problems. When crushing or handling dry slag, wear a dust mask. Keep the area wet to suppress dust. Also, never burn slag or use it in cooking firesâit may release toxic fumes. Educate your community about these risks. Good slag management protects both your health and the environment.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Slag Chemistry and Management in African Smelting Operations

Slag is not waste. In any smelting operation â whether you are running a cupola in Gauteng, a DC arc furnace in the Copperbelt, or an ilmenite smelter in KwaZulu-Natal â slag is a process stream that carries real money. It consumes energy, flux, and refractory; it determines whether your metal separates cleanly; and it either becomes a revenue line or a disposal liability. For African smelters operating on thin margins and volatile power costs, slag chemistry is one of the few levers where a small change in flux ratio or tapping temperature translates directly into cost per tonne of metal.

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into field-ready guidance. It is written for plant managers, metallurgists, and process engineers who need to make decisions on the floor â not in a journal.

Functions of Slag â What You Are Actually Paying For

Slag performs four jobs simultaneously: it collects gangue and oxide impurities, it protects the metal bath from re-oxidation, it controls heat transfer and furnace atmosphere, and it transports impurities out of the furnace. When any of these fail, you see it in metal recovery, refractory wear, or tap-hole blockages. In African copper and PGM smelters, slag typically accounts for 60â80% of the mass leaving the furnace. That mass is heated to 1,200â1,500 Â°C â so every kilogram of unnecessary slag is a kilogram of wasted electricity or coke.

Composition and Properties â The Control Variables

The three levers you control are basicity (usually CaO/SiOâ ratio), FeO content, and temperature. Silica-based slags dominate ferrous and base-metal smelting in Africa; the Copperbelt's historical slag dumps are essentially iron-silicate glass with residual copper. Basic slags (higher CaO) are used where sulphur removal or refractory protection matters. The table below gives typical operating windows.

Table 1: Typical slag compositions and operating parameters for African-relevant smelting routes
Process SiOâ (%) FeO (%) CaO (%) Basicity (CaO/SiOâ) Tap Temp (Â°C)
Copper matte smelting (flash/DC arc) 30â38 35â45 5â12 0.15â0.35 1,200â1,280
PGM smelting (UG2 / Merensky) 38â46 20â30 8â15 0.20â0.35 1,350â1,500
Ilmenite smelting (KZN) 20â28 15â25 (as TiOâ-rich) 2â8 0.10â0.30 1,600â1,700
Ferromanganese (SA) 30â38 5â12 (MnO-rich) 25â40 0.8â1.2 1,400â1,550

Sources: Davenport et al., Extractive Metallurgy of Copper (Elsevier, 2011); Jones, R.T., "Platinum smelting in South Africa," Southern African Pyrometallurgy (SAIMM, 2006); Olsen, Tangstad & Lindstad, Production of Manganese Ferroalloys (Tapir Academic Press, 2007).

Viscosity and Fluidity â The Temperature Trap

Slag viscosity is the single most common cause of operational pain in African smelters, especially where power interruptions force temperature swings. A slag that is fluid at 1,300 Â°C can become a paste at 1,200 Â°C, blocking tap holes and trapping metal droplets. Viscosity is driven by silica content (higher SiOâ = more polymerised = more viscous), FeO content (FeO acts as a network modifier, reducing viscosity), and temperature. Practical rule: keep slag superheat above 50â80 Â°C above liquidus and target FeO high enough to stay fluid without sacrificing metal recovery.

Table 2: Slag viscosity indicators and corrective actions
Observation Likely Cause Corrective Action Cost Impact
Slag "freezes" in tap hole Low superheat; high SiOâ Increase tap temp 30â50 Â°C; add FeO or CaO Extra energy ~5â10% of furnace power
Metal droplets entrained in slag High viscosity; poor settling time Extend settling; adjust basicity; reduce SiOâ Metal loss 0.5â2% of production
Excessive refractory erosion Basicity too high; FeO too aggressive Reduce CaO; consider MgO addition Refractory reline: major capex event
Foaming / furnace instability Gas entrapment; high viscosity Reduce feed rate; check flux sizing Lost production time

Sources: SAIMM Southern African Pyrometallurgy conference proceedings (2006â2020); Mills, K.C., Slag Atlas, 2nd ed. (Verlag Stahleisen, 1995).

MetalâSlag Separation â Where Recovery Is Won or Lost

Separation depends on density difference (matte ~5.0â5.5 g/cmÂ³ vs slag ~2.8â3.5 g/cmÂ³), interfacial tension, and settling time. In practice, African smelters lose metal through three mechanisms: (1) chemically dissolved metal oxide in slag, (2) physically entrained matte droplets, and (3) matte trapped in slag during tapping. The first is unavoidable but controllable through chemistry; the second and third are operational and can be reduced by 30â50% with disciplined tapping and settling practice. In PGM smelting, even 0.5% metal loss in slag represents millions of rand annually.

â  SAFETY WARNING â SLAG TAPPING AND HANDLING

Molten slag at 1,200â1,600 Â°C causes catastrophic burns on contact and can explode when it meets water or damp ground. In African plants, the most common incidents occur during slag tapping, granulation, and ladle transport. Never tap into a wet or damp ladle. Ensure granulation water flow is interlocked and confirmed before tapping. Keep personnel clear of the tap-hole line; wear full aluminised PPE including face shield and spats. Slag dumps can remain hot internally for months â never walk on fresh dump surfaces. Follow mine health and safety regulations (e.g., South Africa's Mine Health and Safety Act, 1996) and site-specific hot-work procedures.

Handling and Utilization â Turning Cost into Revenue

African smelters increasingly treat slag as a product. Common routes:

  • Aggregate and road base: Dense, crystalline slag is crushed and sold to construction. Copperbelt slags have been used in road construction for decades.
  • Cement and concrete: Granulated slag (rapid water quenching) forms a glassy, cementitious material. Slag cement blends are standard in South African construction (SANS 50197).
  • Metal recovery from historical dumps: Old slag dumps in Zambia and DRC contain 0.5â1.5% Cu and are being reprocessed by flotation and leaching. This is a real business line â not a charity project.
  • Railway ballast and abrasives: Where chemistry allows.

The business case is simple: if slag disposal costs USD 15â40 per tonne (transport, landfill fees, environmental compliance), and slag aggregate sells for USD 8â25 per tonne, the swing is USD 25â65 per tonne. For a smelter producing 200,000 tpa of slag, that is USD 5â13 million per year of value either captured or lost.

Environmental Aspects â Compliance Is Non-Negotiable

Slag contains heavy metals (Cu, Pb, Zn, As, Cd) that can leach under acidic conditions. In African jurisdictions, disposal is governed by national environmental regulations â for example, South Africa's National Environmental Management: Waste Act (NEM:WA) and the National Water Act, Zambia's Environmental Management Act, and DRC's Code Minier. Key controls:

  • Leach testing (TCLP or SPLP) before disposal or reuse.
  • Lined or engineered containment for reactive slag.
  • Dust suppression on slag dumps â fine slag dust is a respiratory hazard.
  • Stormwater management to prevent acid drainage from dump runoff.
  • Closure planning and financial provision from day one.

Non-compliance risks fines, licence revocation, and community shutdowns â all of which cost more than doing it right.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Know your target basicity (CaO/SiOâ) and keep it within Â±0.05 of setpoint.
  2. Monitor FeO in slag â target window for fluidity without excessive metal loss.
  3. Maintain superheat of at least 50 Â°C above slag liquidus at tap.
  4. Inspect tap holes every shift; clear blockages immediately.
  5. Never tap into wet ladles or damp ground â verify dryness before tap.
  6. Sample and assay slag at least once per shift for Cu/Ni/PGM loss tracking.
  7. Leach-test slag before any disposal or reuse decision.
  8. Track slag-to-metal ratio as a KPI â it is a direct cost driver.

Further Reading â Free Official Sources

  • SAIMM â Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy: free conference proceedings and technical papers on African smelting practice.
  • Mintek (South Africa): publicly available technical bulletins on pyrometallurgy and slag behaviour.
  • USGS National Minerals Information Center: free commodity and slag production statistics for Africa.
  • International Copper Association: free technical briefs on copper smelting and slag management.
  • US EPA: free guidance on slag leach testing and industrial waste management (TCLP/SPLP methods).

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Smelting Fundamentals. This module is business-first: every technical decision in slag management should be traceable to cost, recovery, or compliance.

quiz.q: What is the main function of slag in smelting?
options: A) To increase metal purity by collecting impurities
B) To add color to the metal
D) To replace coke as fuel
quiz.explanation: Slag collects impurities like silica and sulfur, allowing clean metal to form.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical component of smelting slag?
quiz.explanation: Gold is a valuable metal, not a slag component; slag is made of oxides.

quiz.q: What is the typical melting point range for smelting slags?
quiz.explanation: Most smelting slags melt between 1100Â°C and 1300Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you test if slag is too viscous?
options: A) Dip a wooden stick and see if it coats thickly
quiz.explanation: A thick coating on a stick indicates high viscosity.

quiz.q: What is the effect of adding lime (CaO) to slag?
quiz.explanation: Lime reduces viscosity, making slag more fluid.

quiz.q: Why is metal-slag separation important?
quiz.explanation: Good separation recovers more metal and produces cleaner slag.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to cool hot slag?
options: A) Pour water on it immediately
B) Let it air-cool in a dry pit
D) Stir it with a wet stick
quiz.explanation: Water can cause explosions; air-cooling is safe.

quiz.q: Which of these is a potential use for non-hazardous slag?
quiz.explanation: Crushed slag is used as road base or concrete aggregate.

quiz.q: What environmental risk does slag pose if left exposed?
options: B) Heavy metals can leach into groundwater
quiz.explanation: Rain can leach heavy metals from slag into water sources.

quiz.q: What should you do if slag contains high lead?
options: A) Use it in children's playgrounds
B) Store it in a lined pit away from water
quiz.explanation: Hazardous slag must be contained to prevent leaching.

quiz.q: What is the density of typical molten slag?
quiz.explanation: Slag density is about 2.5â3.0 g/cmÂ³, less than metal.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects slag viscosity?
quiz.explanation: Higher temperature lowers viscosity significantly.

quiz.q: What is a good silica-to-iron ratio for copper smelting slag?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1:1 to 1.5:1 silica to iron is typical for copper slag.

quiz.q: How can you increase slag fluidity without changing composition?
options: D) Stir with a wooden stick
quiz.explanation: Higher temperature reduces viscosity, improving fluidity.

quiz.q: What should you do before tapping slag?
options: A) Let the furnace rest to settle metal
quiz.explanation: A settling period allows metal droplets to sink.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to test slag viscosity in the field?
quiz.explanation: A dry wooden stick dipped in slag shows coating thickness.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor metal-slag separation?
options: A) Shiny metal prills in slag
quiz.explanation: Visible metal prills indicate trapped metal.

quiz.q: Why should you preheat tapping tools?
options: A) To avoid chilling the slag
quiz.explanation: Cold tools can freeze slag, causing blockages.

quiz.q: What is a safe storage method for slag?
options: A) In a dry, covered area
C) In an open pit with water
quiz.explanation: Dry storage prevents leaching and dust.

quiz.q: Which slag component can be used to neutralize acidic soil?
quiz.explanation: Lime in slag raises soil pH.

quiz.q: What is a health risk when handling dry slag?
quiz.explanation: Slag dust can cause lung problems; wear a mask.

quiz.q: How can you reduce slag volume?
quiz.explanation: Proper fluxing reduces excess slag generation.

quiz.q: What should you do with hazardous slag?
options: A) Bury in a lined pit away from water
quiz.explanation: Lined pits prevent leaching of heavy metals.

quiz.q: Which of these is a minor element often found in copper slag?
quiz.explanation: Sulfur is a common minor element in copper smelting slag.

quiz.q: What happens if slag is too thin (low viscosity)?
options: A) It may erode furnace lining
quiz.explanation: Low viscosity slag can splash and corrode refractory.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for slag quality?
options: A) Pan a crushed sample for metal prills
quiz.explanation: Panning reveals trapped metal, indicating poor slag.

quiz.q: Why is slag density important?
options: A) It allows slag to float on metal
quiz.explanation: Lower density makes slag float, enabling separation.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when storing slag long-term?
options: A) Cover it to keep rain out
B) Leave it in the open
quiz.explanation: Covering prevents leaching and dust.

quiz.q: Which gas can be released if slag is heated again?
quiz.explanation: Sulfur in slag can oxidize to SO2 when reheated.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if slag contains over 1% lead?
quiz.explanation: High lead slag is hazardous and must be contained.
